patterns.title: The Hold-Up Problem
patterns.domain: Information, incentive, and commitment problems; relationship-specific investment, incomplete contracts, outside options, and sequential bargaining

sources.title: Benjamin Klein, Robert G. Crawford, and Armen A. Alchian, Vertical Integration, Appropriable Rents, and the Competitive Contracting Process (1978)
sources.supports: Foundational asset specificity, specialized appropriable returns, contracting costs, integration, and long-term enforcement discussion.
sources.read_method: University course-hosted original paper opened and read in full-text extraction: introduction and earlier intellectual lineage, definitions and printing-press example, specificity versus ordinary monopoly rents, integration costs, and long-term explicit/implicit contracting sections.
sources.boundary: Foundational theoretical and institutional account, not an empirical test of Lina’s shop-fit-out scenario. The article does not reproduce the contested Fisher Body historical narrative or claim a single inventor of all hold-up theory. Quasi-rents are distinguished from profit; no numerical quasi-rent estimate is attributed to the paper.

sources.title: Sanford J. Grossman and Oliver D. Hart, The Costs and Benefits of Ownership: A Theory of Vertical and Lateral Integration (1986)
sources.supports: Residual control allocation under incomplete contracts affects ex-ante investment incentives; integration may help one side while weakening the other.
sources.read_method: University-hosted original paper opened and read: abstract, introductory critique of automatic integration remedies, definition of ownership, and two-period model framing separating contractibility, renegotiation, and investment incentives.
sources.boundary: Conditional formal model, not a universal theorem that ownership removes hold-up or an empirical merger recommendation. Lina’s one-sided offer game is a separate original teaching example.

sources.title: Nathan Nunn, Relationship-Specificity, Incomplete Contracts, and the Pattern of Trade (2007; accessible 2005 working paper consulted)
sources.supports: Reported relationship between contract enforcement and specialization in industries requiring relationship-specific inputs. The early full text explains industry proxies, judicial-quality measures, cross-country comparisons, and identification concerns.
sources.read_method: Published Harvard repository metadata/abstract and publisher abstract opened and read. Final-paper downloads failed on author/repository hosts. Original NBER-hosted March 29, 2005 draft opened and read: introduction, model setup, data section, input specificity construction using exchange/reference pricing, subjective rule-of-law measure, and discussion of robustness/endogeneity. Version difference is explicit in the article and bibliography.
sources.boundary: No effect size or causal policy forecast is repeated. The draft’s detailed methods are not silently attributed as a full review of the final publication. Cross-country institutional evidence is not direct observation of all firm-level renegotiation or a proof that integration is best. Proxy and identification assumptions constrain inference.

patterns.short_description: Recognize when a relationship-specific investment weakens later bargaining alternatives, then protect investment incentives through credible terms, portability, or control rights.
use_when: What survives if Lina rejects renewal terms?
goals: Recognize the familiar situation and preserve the defining mechanism.
Distinguish formal assumptions, empirical findings, and hypothetical continuations.
Make intervention authority, opportunity costs, and remaining constraints explicit.
mechanisms: Protect usable outside value or secure credible terms before committing specific investment.
Portability costs more; some fit-out stays sunk. Real alternatives and sufficient returns remain necessary.

example_structure.scenario: Tenant considers specific shop fit-out before unprotected renewal after the initial lease expires. Initial term insufficient alone to recover investment; initial lease is honored. Later strong take-it-or-leave-it offer is a teaching assumption, not tenancy law. Portable fittings cost more but improve a real moving option; some work remains sunk. Anticipation can deter investment without any observed demand; market-wide rent change alone is not appropriation.
example_structure.changed_relationship: Protect usable outside value or secure credible terms before committing specific investment.
example_structure.residual_constraints: Portability costs more; some fit-out stays sunk. Real alternatives and sufficient returns remain necessary.
example_structure.comparison: Qualitative choices, dependencies, and consequences; no invented scores, computed trajectory, or measured improvement claimed.

visual.question: What survives if Lina rejects renewal terms?
visual.alternative_text: Hypothetical qualitative illustration. After location-specific fit-out, the initial lease expires and Orion proposes renewal. Lina can accept or leave with weak outside value for dedicated fixtures. A more costly portable design can preserve a stronger moving option if real premises and affordable relocation exist. Change: Protect usable outside value or secure credible terms before committing specific investment. Limitation: Portability costs more; some fit-out stays sunk. Real alternatives and sufficient returns remain necessary.
visual.caption: Hypothetical illustration. The rejection branch exposes the investment-dependent outside option. Accepting later can be sensible even when the original investment would not repay itself. Portable fittings change the fallback before spending; existing lease obligations remain honored.
